title: Central Limit Theorem Simulator
summary: Two panels on one shared value axis: a population that is nothing like normal, with the most recent sample marked beneath it, and a histogram of the mean of every sample drawn so far. Only the lower panel changes shape, and the theory sits beside the simulation while it does.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a population, one sample from it, and the distribution of a statistic across many samples.
State what the central limit theorem is about, and what it does not claim about the data themselves.
Predict how the standard error changes with sample size, and check the prediction against a simulation.
Explain why a rule such as thirty is enough depends on the population it is applied to.
Recognise that rescaling a picture of the means changes how wide they look and nothing about how wide they are.
interactionTypes: two-panel figure on one shared value axis
sample-size manipulation that clears and rebuilds the pile
theory beside simulation, row by row
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Every value is generated and discarded in the browser.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. The three objects in the figure differ by mark as well as by colour: the population is a filled curve, one sample is a row of ticks, and the means are a histogram, and each is named in text inside the figure. The figure carries a description that is rewritten on every change, stating the population, the sample size, how many means have been drawn and their centre and spread against the predicted standard error. Every plotted quantity also appears in the table beneath, which shows the theoretical value beside the measured one. The axis states in words whether the two panels share a scale. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Simulated. Both populations are mathematical distributions with exactly known moments, so the predicted column is not an estimate. No real dataset is used and no figure here is an empirical finding.
simulationNotes: Randomness is seeded with mulberry32, using Box-Muller normals and inverse-CDF exponentials, and the stream position is folded into the seed so a given seed and settings reproduce the same run however it is broken into presses. The skewed population is 20 plus an exponential with mean 20, giving mu 40, sigma 20 and skewness 2. The bimodal population is half Normal(30, 6) and half Normal(70, 6), giving mu 50 and sigma the square root of 436, with skewness 0. Predictions for the mean of n draws are mu for the centre, sigma over the square root of n for the standard error, and population skewness over the square root of n for the skewness. Changing the population, the sample size or the seed clears the accumulated means, because means drawn under other settings are not comparable.
readmeTopic: sampling distributions, the central limit theorem and what it does not claim about data
